title: Showing the World
summary: Bell had a talking machine, but almost nobody believed in it yet. So he showed it off: to an emperor at a giant fair, to crowds in lecture halls, and even to Queen Victoria in her palace. Soon people were renting telephones in pairs and stringing wires between their homes and shops.

sections.heading: A Giant Fair for a Birthday
paragraphs: In 1876 the United States turned 100 years old. To celebrate the centennial, the hundredth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, the city of Philadelphia held an enormous fair called the Centennial Exhibition. It was the first official world's fair ever held in the United States.

Imagine walking through the gates in Fairmount Park, beside the Schuylkill River. The fair ran from May 10 to November 10, 1876, and covered a huge area with more than 200 buildings inside a fence nearly 5 kilometres (3 miles) long. The Main Exhibition Building alone was about 573 metres (1,880 feet) long, one of the biggest buildings in the world at the time. Around 10 million visitors came, at a time when the whole country had only about 46 million people. Dozens of nations sent displays.

The star of the fair was a gigantic steam engine called the Corliss Centennial Engine. It stood about 14 metres (45 feet) tall, could produce about 1,400 horsepower, and powered rows and rows of machines in Machinery Hall through long spinning belts and shafts. On opening day, President Ulysses S. Grant and the Emperor of Brazil, Dom Pedro II, started it together. Visitors could also see typewriters, new kinds of sewing machines, the right arm and torch of the future Statue of Liberty, and all kinds of telegraph equipment.

Somewhere in this sea of machines, among the displays about science and education, was a small exhibit by a Boston teacher named Alexander Graham Bell. It did not look like much: a few odd instruments, some wire, and a box or two. Most visitors walked straight past it.

Bell almost did not go at all. He was busy with his teaching in Boston, and his students had exams coming up. A well-known family story says that Mabel Hubbard, the young woman he hoped to marry, more or less tricked him onto the train to Philadelphia, and that he was annoyed with her until he realised she was right. Like many family stories, it may have grown a little in the retelling, but it is clear that Bell's backers, including Mabel's father Gardiner Greene Hubbard, wanted him at the fair. They knew that a single good demonstration in front of the right people could be worth more than months of work alone in a laboratory.

sections.heading: The Emperor Picks Up the Receiver
paragraphs: Every big fair had judges who walked from exhibit to exhibit to decide which inventions deserved awards. On Sunday, June 25, 1876, a hot summer day, the judges for electrical inventions reached Bell's table. They had been working for hours and were tired, and some accounts say they were ready to call it a day.

Among them were two very unusual judges. One was Sir William Thomson, the brilliant Scottish-Irish physicist who had helped make the transatlantic telegraph cable work, as you read in Part 4. He would later become Lord Kelvin. The other was Dom Pedro II, the Emperor of Brazil, who was touring the United States and was fascinated by science and education. According to many accounts, the emperor had already met Bell earlier that year in Boston, because he was interested in Bell's work teaching deaf students.

Standing nearby was another visitor with a special interest: Elisha Gray, whose caveat had reached the Patent Office on the same day as Bell's application. Gray was exhibiting his own telegraph inventions at the fair.

Bell's instruments had to be adjusted carefully, and it took some fiddling to get them working. The transmitter and receiver were placed some distance apart so the judges could be sure the sound was really coming through the wire. Bell went to the transmitter and spoke. Thomson listened at the receiver, and so did the emperor.

Thomson later reported that he heard Bell say “To be or not to be,” the famous line from Shakespeare's play Hamlet, and even the words that follow in the play, “there's the rub.” The sound was faint, but the words were there. Dom Pedro is said to have exclaimed something like “My God, it talks!” That quotation is repeated in many books, but nobody wrote it down at the moment, so we should treat it as a lively story rather than a certain fact.

What is certain is that the judges were deeply impressed. Bell's telephone received one of the exhibition's awards, and Thomson became one of its strongest early supporters. When he returned to Britain, he described the telephone at the meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in Glasgow in September 1876, which was one of the first times it was presented to a British scientific audience. When a world-famous scientist like Thomson said the talking wire was real, other scientists started paying attention.

sections.heading: Voices Along the Fence Posts in Ontario
paragraphs: Talking from one end of a hall to another was one thing. But could a voice travel between towns? That summer, Bell set out to find out, and he did it in Canada.

Bell's parents lived on a farm at Tutela Heights, just outside the town of Brantford, Ontario. The family had moved there from Britain in 1870, as you read in Part 6. In the summer of 1876, Bell visited and began testing his telephone over longer wires. In one test, wire was strung along the tops of fences from Mount Pleasant Road to his father's house, with a receiver set up on the porch. Many years later, Bell remembered simply that it “worked.”

The most famous test came on August 10, 1876. Bell arranged to use a real telegraph line belonging to the Dominion Telegraph Company. The transmitter, with its batteries, was in Brantford. The receiver was in the town of Paris, Ontario, about 13 kilometres (8 miles) away, in the company's telegraph office, which was inside a shoe store owned by a man named Robert White. Bell himself is usually described as listening at the Paris end.

Picture the scene in the little shop in Paris: shelves of boots, a telegraph desk, and a small group of curious people crowding around a strange instrument. Then, out of the receiver, came voices from Brantford: people speaking, reading aloud and singing songs. By most accounts, some of the voices belonged to Bell's own relatives, including his father and his uncle.

This was a one-way call. People in Paris could hear Brantford, but they could not answer back through the telephone, because of how the equipment and batteries were set up. Even so, it is often called the world's first long-distance telephone call. Today a plaque in Paris remembers the event.

Two months later, in October 1876, Bell and Watson managed a true two-way conversation over a telegraph wire between Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, a few kilometres apart. They talked back and forth for hours and wrote down what they heard to check it. Now the telephone was not just sending sounds. It was letting two people have a conversation.

sections.heading: Professor Bell Takes the Stage
paragraphs: In the 1870s there was no television, no radio and no internet. If people wanted to learn about the latest science, they often bought a ticket to a public lecture. Famous speakers travelled from town to town, and crowds packed into halls to watch experiments on stage. Bell, who was a skilled speaker and teacher, realised this was the perfect way to show off the telephone, and to earn some money, which he badly needed.

The most famous of these lectures took place on the evening of February 12, 1877, at Lyceum Hall in Salem, Massachusetts. More than 500 people paid to see Professor Bell. On the stage was a telephone connected by a telegraph wire to Boston, roughly 25 kilometres (16 miles) away, where Thomas Watson was waiting at the other end.

Bell explained how sound and electricity worked, and then the show began. Voices came out of the telephone from Boston. Watson, who was not a trained singer but had a strong, loud voice, sang songs down the line so that the audience could hear. The early telephones were so faint that Watson had to shout and sing as loudly as he could, and the people in the hall leaned forward in silence to catch the sounds.

That night also made newspaper history. A local man named Henry Batchelder, who wrote reports for the Boston Globe, used the telephone to dictate his story about the lecture to a Globe reporter in Boston. The next day the newspaper printed it, and it is often described as the first news report ever sent by telephone.

Bell and Watson gave more lectures in other New England cities and in New York during 1877. Each demonstration followed a similar plan: Bell on stage explaining, Watson far away singing, talking, or playing an instrument such as a cornet or an organ, and the audience amazed that sounds could arrive from a distant city. Some people even suspected a trick, wondering if a singer was hidden backstage.

These shows did more than entertain. Every newspaper report about them was free advertising. Business owners in the audience began to imagine how useful it would be to talk to a warehouse, a factory or a home without sending a messenger boy running through the streets.

sections.heading: A Queen on the Line
paragraphs: Bell also took the telephone across the Atlantic. He had received a British patent on December 9, 1876, and in the summer of 1877 he travelled to Britain, where he stayed for more than a year, giving demonstrations and trying to start a telephone business there.

His most famous British audience was Queen Victoria herself. On the evening of January 14, 1878, Bell was invited to Osborne House, the Queen's seaside home on the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast. In a grand room called the Council Room, he set up his instruments, helped by two assistants, Colonel W. H. Reynolds and Charlton Wollaston. The Queen was joined by her daughter Princess Beatrice and her son the Duke of Connaught.

The demonstration ran from about half past nine at night until around midnight. Wires connected Osborne House to several places. At nearby Osborne Cottage, the home of Sir Thomas Biddulph, one of the Queen's officials, Sir Thomas and Lady Biddulph spoke with the Queen, and the American journalist Kate Field, a friend and supporter of Bell, sang songs into the telephone. At Cowes, an army officer, Major Webber of the Royal Engineers, was on the line, and in Southampton, William Preece, a senior engineer of the British Post Office, which ran the country's telegraphs, took part. Most amazing of all, a line was connected to London, nearly 130 kilometres (80 miles) away, where a Mr Wilmot played an organ and the listeners at Osborne could hear the music.

Not everything worked perfectly, and the sound was often faint. The early phones used in the demonstration had a single opening that served as both mouthpiece and earpiece, so people had to keep moving it from their mouth to their ear and back again.

Queen Victoria wrote about the evening in her journal. She described the sound as rather faint and noted that you had to hold the tube close to your ear. One of the actual telephones used at Osborne Cottage that night survives today in the collection of the Science Museum Group in Britain. The demonstration was reported in The Times newspaper, and having a queen try your invention was the kind of publicity no advertisement could buy.

sections.heading: A Company and a Wedding in the Same Week
paragraphs: Back in the United States, July 1877 turned out to be one of the most important months of Bell's life.

On July 9, 1877, Gardiner Greene Hubbard organised the Bell Telephone Company in Boston. It was built around one thing: Bell's patent, No. 174,465. The company was divided into 5,000 shares, which are pieces of ownership. Bell received 1,497 shares. Thomas Sanders, the Salem leather merchant who had paid for much of Bell's research, also received 1,497 and became the company's treasurer. Hubbard and his family held about 1,500, and Hubbard acted as the company's leader. Thomas Watson, who was only 23 years old, received 499 shares and was put in charge of making the telephones. Not bad for a young mechanic who had started out building other people's gadgets in a Boston workshop.

Two days later, on July 11, 1877, Alexander Graham Bell married Mabel Hubbard at her parents' home in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Mabel was 19. She had been deaf since a serious illness, scarlet fever, when she was about five years old, and she had become an excellent lip-reader. She was clever, practical and confident, and she would become one of Bell's most important partners in everything he did.

Bell's wedding present to his bride was remarkable. He gave her all but 10 of his 1,497 shares in the new telephone company. At that moment nobody knew whether the shares would ever be worth much. Within a few years they made the family wealthy.

Soon after the wedding, the couple set off for Britain on a long honeymoon that was also a working trip, which is how Bell came to be demonstrating telephones to Queen Victoria in January 1878. Their first daughter, Elsie May Bell, was born in London in May 1878.

sections.heading: The $100,000 Offer and the Memo That Never Was
paragraphs: You may have heard a famous story about the telegraph giant Western Union. It goes like this: Bell's side offered to sell the telephone patent to Western Union for $100,000, and the company's experts wrote a scornful memo saying the telephone was a useless toy with too many problems to ever be taken seriously. It is a great story about how even experts can be wrong. But the memo part almost certainly is not true.
Let's sort out what really happened and what did not.

The offer itself may well be real. Thomas Watson, writing many years later, remembered that in the autumn of 1876 Hubbard offered to sell the rights to Bell's patents to William Orton, the president of Western Union, for $100,000, and that the offer was turned down. Watson's memory is the main source for this, so historians treat it with some caution, but it fits with what else we know. Another documented episode involves Chauncey Depew, a well-known New York lawyer. Hubbard offered him a one-sixth share in the telephone for $10,000. Depew asked Orton for advice, Orton told him the telephone had no future, and Depew stayed out. Depew later joked about how much money he had missed.

The memo is a different matter. Researchers who have searched for it have found no trace of it in newspapers from 1876 to 1900, or in any documents from the period. The earliest known printed version appeared in 1968 in an engineering journal, where the writer said he had put it together from two similar versions he had come across. As early as 1976, an article in the engineering magazine IEEE Spectrum called it suspect. So it is best to think of the famous memo as a modern joke or legend, not a real historical document.

What Western Union actually did is even more interesting. It did not think the telephone was worthless for long. In 1877, once the telephone started to catch on, Western Union bought up rival telephone patents, including ones from Elisha Gray and Amos Dolbear, hired Thomas Edison to design a better transmitter, and set up its own telephone business to compete with Bell. That set the stage for a huge legal battle, which you will read about in Part 10.

sections.heading: Renting Telephones in Pairs
paragraphs: So how did you actually get a telephone in 1877? You could not walk into a shop and buy one. And you could not call just anyone, because there was no network yet. There were no telephone exchanges, no operators and no phone numbers.

Instead, Hubbard made a smart business decision: telephones would be rented, never sold. The company kept ownership of every instrument. Customers paid a yearly fee to use them, and the company would repair them for free. This gave the company steady income and control over how its telephones were used.

In May 1877, Hubbard put out a printed circular, a kind of advertising leaflet, that is often called the first telephone advertisement. It offered pairs of telephones for connecting two places “not more than twenty miles apart.” Renting two telephones to connect a home with another building cost $20 a year. For business use it cost $40 a year, paid every six months in advance. Each extra telephone on the same line was $10 more, and a louder call signal cost $5. If you did not already have a wire, the company could arrange to build a line for about $100 to $150 per mile. Orders were to be sent to Thomas A. Watson at 109 Court Street in Boston.

Notice the word pairs. Each early telephone line was a private line connecting exactly two places, such as a banker's home and his bank, a factory office and its warehouse, or a doctor's house and a pharmacy. If you wanted to talk to three places, you needed three separate lines, each with its own pair of telephones. One of the first private lines in the Boston area is often said to have connected the workshop of Charles Williams Jr., where Bell's telephones were made, to Williams's home.

What did one of these rented telephones look like? Many were simple wooden boxes or handheld wooden tubes, with a round opening at one end. Inside was a permanent magnet, a coil of wire and a thin iron diaphragm. These instruments did not need a battery at all. When you spoke into one, your voice shook the iron diaphragm near the magnet, and that movement created a tiny electric current in the coil all by itself. At the other end, the same kind of instrument turned the current back into sound. The same opening was used for talking and listening, so a conversation meant a lot of moving the telephone up to your mouth, then over to your ear, then back again.

Because the current came only from the speaker's voice, these telephones were quiet, and they worked best over short distances. There was also no proper ringing bell on the earliest models. To get the attention of the person at the other end, you might tap on the diaphragm or shout into the instrument and hope someone was close enough to hear. That is why the company offered a separate, louder call signal for an extra fee. It would take several more years of inventing, including new transmitters and proper ringers, before telephones became loud, clear and easy to use. Even so, people were willing to put up with the awkwardness, because being able to speak to someone in another building, instantly, felt almost like magic.

Even with these limits, the numbers grew quickly. By July 31, 1877, only weeks after the company was formed, 778 telephones had been rented out. By the end of 1877, more than 5,000 Bell telephones were in use. By the end of July 1878, the number was over 12,000, and by early 1879 it was about 22,000. By around 1880, there were tens of thousands of telephones in the United States, roughly 50,000 by common estimates, and the number was still climbing fast.

But wires running only between two places could not last. As more and more people got telephones, the tangle of private lines would have become impossible. In January 1878, the first commercial telephone exchange opened in New Haven, Connecticut, letting subscribers be connected to one another. That story belongs to Part 11.

First, though, there is a mystery we have been tiptoeing around since Part 6. What is really happening inside a telephone? How does a human voice, made of nothing but moving air, actually turn into electricity, rush down a wire, and turn back into a voice at the other end?

deepDive: The years 1876 to 1878 show that inventing a device and launching a technology are different achievements. The Centennial demonstration of June 25, 1876, mattered less for its technical quality, which was poor (Thomson heard fragments of Hamlet only after much adjustment, and another judge heard little), than for its witnesses. William Thomson's endorsement carried enormous scientific weight, and his report to the British Association in Glasgow in September 1876 introduced the telephone to British science. The Ontario trials of August 1876 established that speech could survive real telegraph lines over about 13 km, though the Brantford–Paris link was one-way; the October 1876 Boston–Cambridge test showed two-way conversation. The 1877 lecture tour, beginning with the Salem lecture of February 12, combined fundraising with publicity; Boston Globe coverage, including the first news dispatch transmitted by telephone, spread the idea widely. The business model was equally important. Hubbard's decision to lease rather than sell instruments, borrowed from his earlier legal work for a shoe-machinery company that leased its machines, gave the Bell interests continuous revenue and control of equipment, a policy that shaped the Bell System for about a century. The May 1877 circular priced pairs of instruments at $20 a year for social use and $40 for business use. Growth was rapid: 778 instruments leased by July 31, 1877; 5,491 by year end; about 22,000 by March 1879. The often-repeated Western Union 'toy' memo deserves scepticism. No version has been found in newspapers from 1876 to 1900 or in documents through 1950; the earliest known printing is from 1968, in an engineering journal. The $100,000 offer rests mainly on Thomas Watson's later recollection. What is documented is that Western Union, after initially declining, moved quickly into the telephone business in 1877 by acquiring patents from Gray and Dolbear and commissioning Edison's transmitter work, a decision that led directly to the patent litigation settled in 1879.
funFact: One of the actual telephones used at Osborne Cottage on the night of Bell's demonstration for Queen Victoria in January 1878 survives today in the collection of Britain's Science Museum Group.
